item.title: Chart of the day: 10-year Treasury yields hit reverse this week but the real test is still ahead
item.description:
Seeing as to how the bond market is faring to end the week, you probably wouldn't have guessed that we actually got hotter-than-expected inflation data from both the US CPI and PPI reports in the past few days. In fact, you might even think it was the opposite. Yet, here we are.

10-year Treasury yields are down to 5.09%, poised for back-to-back weekly declines for the first time since June. That is certainly keeping things interesting with yields tumbling back to draw in the 5.00% mark again as broader market sentiment turns more cautious.

The rejection this week at 5.30% following the US CPI report stands out rather clearly, with yields failing to sustain a break higher before retreating sharply. And that now puts the spotlight back on the 5.00% level, which had previously played the role in keeping yields from breaking out back in September.

As such, it would require a firm daily close below 5.00% to deliver a stronger signal that the recent upward momentum is starting to unravel.

After which, that could open up a move towards 4.70%, where the 100-day moving average (red line) is also sticking nearby at 4.73%. Further below, the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 4.50% could come into consideration.

But for now, it's baby steps first. I wouldn't be too quick to call an end to the broader uptrend just yet.

10-year yields are still comfortably holding above the key 5.00% threshold in the past few sessions. And any semblance of a rebound back towards 5.20% or even 5.30% again would put the recent rejection back to the test.

And from a fundamental standpoint, nothing much has really changed. Inflation pressures are still holding up and the same structural factors underpinning yields since last month are also still very much in place. Heavy Treasury issuance and concerns about the long-term trajectory of US debt are key reasons why investors are demanding more compensation to hold longer-dated government bonds.

But at least for the time being, all eyes are turning back to the 5.00% mark as the line in the sand. Hold above and we're still talking about the upward pressure in yields being sustained for the most part. But break below, and this could turn the sharp pullback this week into something more meaningful perhaps.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold shrugs off hot inflation data as market focus may be shifting to growth concerns
item.description:
Yesterday, US PPI came in much higher than expected, but gold's reaction was similar to what we saw after the US CPI release, that is the price initially spiked lower before recovering and rallying to new highs. Treasury yields also fell following the data, pointing to either overstretched positioning or growing concerns about the economic outlook.

Despite the Core PCE estimates now showing a monthly increase of 0.34% in October, the rate hike expectations for October actually fell after the PPI release. What’s more interesting is that further out the curve, we’ve seen a dovish repricing.

On the geopolitical front, we haven’t seen any change. The Saudi Arabia–Houthi conflict continues, while US–Iran negotiations remain at a stalemate. Meanwhile, oil prices continue to rise amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

Looking ahead, we have the Flash PMIs, the FOMC, the US-Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections as key catalysts. If the economic data starts pointing to deteriorating economic conditions, then we could see the market starting to price in an economic slowdown, which could initially support gold.

If the data continues to support strong economic momentum, though, then we could see the precious metal coming back under pressure, unless the Fed continues to stay more dovish than market’s expectations, as that would lower real yields and support gold.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) is finally approaching the downward trendline. The sellers will likely lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into the 3,885 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the 4,700 level next, with the 4,500 level as the first target.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a strong resistance zone around the 4,228 level. If the price probes above the trendline, the resistance will likely be the last line of defence for the sellers. From a risk management perspective, the sellers will likely step in around the trendline and the resistance, with a defined risk above the resistance, to position for new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking above the resistance to open the door for new highs and target the 4,400 level next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. The buyers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs and target a break above the resistance. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to increase the bearish bets into new lows, targeting the 3,885 level next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

item.title: Dow Jones futures analysis: Fed risks and key levels for October 16
item.description:
Dow Jones futures recover, but can bulls overcome 52,612 amid Fed and inflation uncertainty?

Dow Jones futures are showing a more constructive technical picture on Friday, October 16, but the economic backdrop remains complicated. Federal Reserve uncertainty, persistent inflation, concerns about AI financing and changing bond-market expectations could influence the next move. Meanwhile, E-mini Dow futures are approaching an important resistance test around 52,612, with higher potential targets if buyers can sustain the recovery. Let's first jump into my Dow Jones futures technical analysis video right with the European market open:

What news could affect the Dow Jones today?

Several developments over the past 24 hours deserve attention. They do not necessarily explain every movement in Dow futures, but they help establish the conditions under which the technical recovery is taking place.

1. Fed Chair Warsh sounds optimistic but offers little interest-rate guidance

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh struck a relatively optimistic tone about the resilience of the US economy during Friday's remarks at the IMF meetings in Bangkok.

However, he avoided signaling what the Fed might do at its upcoming October 27-28 meeting or its December meeting.

This matters because the Fed raised its policy rate in September, while recent inflation readings have increased uncertainty about whether further tightening will be required.

As Eamonn Sheridan explains in Warsh won't prejudge rest of 2026, names October and December as decision points, the absence of clear guidance leaves investors more dependent on incoming economic data.

What could this mean for the Dow?

A resilient economy would generally support corporate revenue and earnings. But if the Fed keeps interest rates elevated, borrowing costs could remain a burden for businesses and consumers.

For traders, the important question is not simply whether Warsh sounds optimistic. It is whether economic resilience can continue without requiring monetary policy that becomes increasingly restrictive.

2. Inflation is becoming a corporate earnings question

Thursday's US Producer Price Index report showed producer prices rising 1.3% in September, the largest monthly increase since March 2022. Annual producer inflation reached 6.3%.

Meanwhile, retail sales rose 0.8% in September, apparently signaling a healthy consumer.

However, there is an important qualification.

Much of the headline retail-sales increase reflected higher gasoline spending. The closely watched retail-sales control group, which excludes several volatile categories, increased just 0.1%.

Furthermore, retail-sales figures are not adjusted for inflation. Spending more money does not necessarily mean consumers are buying more goods.

For the Dow, this creates two related risks.

First, companies could face higher transportation, energy and production costs. Second, customers may become more selective about what they buy.

Home Depot, Walmart and other consumer-facing businesses could feel the consequences differently, depending on their customers, pricing power and product mix.

Justin Low explains the underlying business problem in today's investingLive educational article, Why higher inflation doesn't always mean bigger corporate profits.

The takeaway for investors: During earnings season, revenue growth alone may not tell the full story. Sales volumes and operating margins could become more revealing, particularly if companies are struggling to pass higher costs on to customers.

3. Falling Treasury yields are not necessarily good news for stocks

One of the more interesting developments this week has been the behavior of the US bond market.

Despite stronger-than-expected inflation figures, Treasury yields have declined from their earlier highs.

Ordinarily, investors might expect inflation surprises to push yields higher as markets anticipate tighter monetary policy.

But another interpretation deserves consideration.

What if bond investors are becoming increasingly concerned that high borrowing costs and persistent inflation could eventually damage economic growth?

In today's analysis of whether the bond market is becoming more concerned about growth than inflation, Justin Low explores precisely that possibility.

This distinction matters for Dow investors.

Lower bond yields can support stock valuations by reducing discount rates and financing costs. However, when yields decline because investors are seeking safety or anticipating weaker economic activity, the implications for corporate earnings may be less favorable.

The useful distinction is why yields are falling, rather than merely whether they are falling.

For example, Caterpillar could benefit from easing financing conditions while simultaneously facing weaker equipment demand if businesses reduce investment.

These opposing influences help explain why the same economic development can have different effects across Dow constituents.

4. AI infrastructure demand remains strong, but financing concerns persist

Another development worth following comes from Europe.

On October 16, Schneider Electric raised its 2026 organic revenue-growth forecast to 12%-14%, citing strong demand for data-center infrastructure. Reuters reported that the company experienced triple-digit growth in data-center demand during the quarter.

That is encouraging evidence that physical infrastructure investment remains strong.

At the same time, recent concern about debt-financed AI expansion is raising questions about whether every company participating in the investment boom will achieve sufficient profitability.

For Dow constituents such as Nvidia and Microsoft, the distinction is important.

AI infrastructure demand can remain strong even while investors become more cautious about the financing, profitability and valuations of certain companies.

These are not necessarily contradictory signals.

Investors could watch whether strong orders continue to translate into sustainable revenue and cash flow, and whether financing concerns remain concentrated in highly leveraged businesses or begin affecting larger investment programs.

5. Oil and Middle East developments remain another source of uncertainty

Oil is particularly relevant because energy costs have contributed heavily to the latest inflation readings.

President Trump said he would rule out certain military actions against Iran while leaving the possibility of other strikes open.

As investingLive reported in Trump draws two red lines on Iran but keeps Pickaxe Mountain strike in play, uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz remains relevant to oil supply.

For the Dow, an escalation that materially increases energy costs could affect manufacturers, consumer spending and interest-rate expectations.

Conversely, sustained easing in oil supply risks could relieve some of those pressures, even if the broader inflation problem remains unresolved.

Why the Dow can behave differently from the broader stock market

There is another point worth remembering when interpreting these developments.

Unlike the market-capitalization-weighted S&P 500, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is price-weighted.

This means a stock with a higher share price generally has a larger percentage influence on the Dow than a lower-priced stock, regardless of the relative size of their companies.

As a result, strength in selected higher-priced constituents can support the Dow even when weakness develops elsewhere in the market.

That does not make the recovery insignificant. It does mean that traders should distinguish the Dow's index performance from the underlying health of the broader equity market.

Watching how industrial, financial, consumer and technology constituents respond to the same news can offer useful confirmation or reveal important divergences.

Dow Jones futures technical analysis: Buyers have improved their position

In my accompanying technical-analysis video, I examine the CBOT E-mini Dow Jones futures (YM) on the four-hour chart.

The technical observations reflect the European morning of October 16, with futures around 52,527 at approximately 09:29 Berlin time.

These are futures prices, not prices for the cash Dow Jones Industrial Average. The latest completed four-hour candle ended at 08:00 Berlin time, while the following candle was still developing.

A breakout, a retracement and a developing bullish recovery

The four-hour structure has improved noticeably.

Following lows around 50,859 on October 1 and 50,909 on October 8, futures began developing a recovery within a rising channel.

The chart also shows a breakout from a smaller corrective structure resembling a bullish flag, followed by a pullback that came close to retesting the breakout area.

That sequence is important.

A breakout on its own can attract buying, but the subsequent pullback provides additional information about whether buyers are willing to defend their earlier progress.

The October 14 decline toward 51,600 failed to develop into another test of the early-October lows. Instead, buyers reasserted themselves and futures recovered toward 52,500 by Friday's European morning.

The latest price structure therefore looks more constructive than it did earlier in the month.

However, an improving recovery is not the same as a confirmed breakout through overhead resistance.

Volume improves the bullish case, but there is an important qualification

The recovery has not occurred on insignificant trading activity.

A strong October 15 four-hour recovery candle traded approximately 45,500 futures contracts, exceeding the volume of comparable four-hour periods on October 13 and 14.

Momentum also improved, with the MACD moving above its signal line on October 15.

These observations suggest that buyers have recently become more effective.

But there is an important contrast.

The October 13 advance toward 52,612 also attracted substantial trading activity before sellers reversed the move.

In other words, both the earlier rejection and the subsequent recovery occurred with meaningful participation.

High trading volume shows activity. It does not, by itself, establish which side will ultimately prevail.

That brings us to the most important technical question for today.

Dow Jones futures: Key levels to watch

52,612: The previous rejection high

On October 13, futures reached approximately 52,612 before reversing sharply.

That level now represents the first important test of the recovery.

Buyers would strengthen their case by establishing a completed four-hour breakout above the previous high, followed by sustained trading above it or a successful retest.

A temporary move above resistance that quickly reverses would provide substantially less confirmation.

There is also a useful volatility consideration.

From the 09:29 snapshot around 52,527, the distance to 52,612 is only about 85 points. Recent four-hour average true range, a measure of trading volatility, was approximately 218 points.

Consequently, a brief move through 52,612 could occur within an otherwise ordinary four-hour trading range.

That makes the reaction after the initial test particularly important.

52,700 and 52,950: Potential bullish objectives

If the recovery continues and buyers overcome the previous rejection area, the technical map identifies two possible upside objectives.

52,700: The first potential bullish objective beyond the October 13 high.

52,950: A higher objective that also aligns with a significant historical trading-activity reference.

These levels are not predictions or automatic buy signals.

For traders already holding a profitable long position, they can serve as areas where partial profit-taking or reassessment may be considered, depending on the individual trading plan.

The important condition is that buyers first demonstrate sufficient strength to overcome the nearby resistance.

52,300-52,450: The first area for buyers to defend

If futures pull back instead of breaking higher, the 52,300-52,450 region is an initial support area worth monitoring.

Holding this area would suggest that buyers are still defending much of the recent recovery.

A sustained decline through it would weaken the immediate bullish picture and raise the possibility of a deeper retracement.

52,263: A previous trading-value reference

The video also highlights an important level near 52,263, associated with the value area of an earlier consolidation.

A value area represents a price region where a substantial share of trading occurred during a selected period.

Why does this matter?

When price moves back into a previous area of heavy trading, it can indicate that the market is revisiting prices where buyers and sellers previously found relatively broad agreement.

This does not automatically mean a reversal is coming.

However, it would be less encouraging for bulls than continued acceptance at higher prices.

52,150: A deeper swing-trading reference

Another level highlighted in the video is the four-hour 20-period exponential moving average, near 52,150 at the time of the analysis.

An exponential moving average gives greater weight to recent prices and can help traders evaluate the direction of a developing trend.

For a swing-trading perspective, I discuss using two consecutive completed four-hour candles below this reference as a more meaningful warning that the recovery is weakening, rather than reacting immediately to one isolated move below it.

That is a confirmation approach, not a guarantee. It may filter out temporary weakness, but it can also identify a reversal later than an earlier warning would.

If that broader support structure deteriorates, the 52,000-52,100 region becomes another relevant area to reassess.

What would strengthen or weaken the bullish outlook?

Bullish continuation

A completed four-hour move above 52,612, followed by sustained trading above the previous rejection area, would provide stronger confirmation that buyers have overcome an important obstacle.

That would increase the relevance of the 52,700 and 52,950 upside objectives.

An inconclusive breakout

A short-lived move above 52,612 that quickly returns below the prior high would be less convincing.

This would suggest that sellers remain active near resistance and that the recovery may require further consolidation.

A weakening recovery

Failure to defend 52,300-52,450, followed by deterioration near 52,263 and 52,150, would progressively weaken the bullish technical interpretation.

A deeper decline toward 52,000-52,100 would raise further questions about whether the recent advance is sustainable.

These scenarios describe areas to evaluate, not instructions that a trade must be placed at any particular price.

What could change the outlook during Friday's US session?

The latest macroeconomic uncertainty makes today's US economic releases particularly relevant.

Three developments deserve attention:

  • 14:30 Berlin time (08:30 New York): US import and export prices. Additional evidence of whether international pricing pressures are feeding into domestic inflation.

  • 15:15 Berlin time (09:15 New York): US industrial production and capacity utilization. A useful check on manufacturing activity and demand for industrial capacity.

  • Travelers (TRV) third-quarter results: Scheduled before the US market opens, with its earnings conference call at 15:00 Berlin time (09:00 New York). The insurer's results could provide a separate, company-specific influence on the price-weighted Dow.

The combination of these releases, Fed uncertainty and the technical resistance test creates several possible paths for Friday's US session.

A constructive industrial-production report accompanied by moderating inflation pressures could support confidence in the economic outlook.

Conversely, renewed inflation pressure or evidence of weakening industrial demand could complicate the recovery.

An especially informative outcome would be how Dow futures respond if the economic news appears favorable but price still fails to overcome 52,612.

That would suggest that improving macroeconomic sentiment has not yet translated into sufficient buying strength at the chart's key resistance.

The takeaway for Dow Jones traders and investors

Dow Jones futures have made meaningful technical progress.

The breakout, subsequent pullback and recovery toward 52,500 suggest that buyers are becoming more effective, and the market has so far avoided revisiting the early-October lows.

But the next test matters more than simply celebrating the recent advance.

The 52,612-52,700 region is where the bullish recovery needs to demonstrate that it can overcome previous selling pressure.

The macroeconomic picture adds another layer of uncertainty. Inflation remains elevated, the Fed is avoiding firm guidance, AI financing concerns have not disappeared and lower Treasury yields may reflect more than one economic interpretation.

For traders, the immediate question is whether futures can break resistance and hold recovered ground. For longer-term investors, the broader issue is whether corporate earnings and economic activity remain resilient under relatively restrictive financial conditions.

The same news can produce different market reactions depending on what investors were expecting beforehand.

That is why I would pay particular attention to how futures respond at the identified technical levels rather than assuming that any single headline must produce a predetermined outcome.

Technical levels reflect the October 16, 2026 morning snapshot, not continuously updated quotes. Futures trading involves risk, and the levels discussed are for educational analysis.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: Equities find some footing after a volatile week
item.description:
• Eurostoxx +0.5%
  • Germany DAX +0.7%
  • France CAC 40 -0.2%
  • UK FTSE 100 -0.2%
  • Spain IBEX +0.5%
  • Italy FTSE MIB +0.6%

European equities are finding some relief today, with most major indices posting modest gains as we approach the end of what has been a rather volatile trading week. The French benchmark index is the notable laggard, with fiscal risks continuing to weigh this week.

For now though, I wouldn't read too much into the early advance just yet. Broader markets have had plenty to digest in trading this week, not least with hotter-than-expected US inflation data from both the CPI and PPI reports. That continues to pose fresh questions on the Fed outlook as well as the bond market selloff, even though there is a much calmer tone in the latter in the past few sessions.

While there Treasury yields and the dollar have eased a fair bit, that doesn't necessarily mean investors are out of the woods. The bigger concern remains that inflation pressures are proving to be more stubborn than hoped, leaving central banks with less room to support growth if economic conditions start to deteriorate. And that will be especially difficult for European stocks to navigate through, given the region's own economic and fiscal challenges.

The overall market mood today is at least helped by a steadier showing in US futures. The late recovery in tech shares overnight is carrying over a little, with S&P 500 futures up 0.1% and Nasdaq futures keeping little changed.

Still, I would be cautious about labelling this as a proper turnaround. European stocks are just about managing to find their feet again but whether they can stay on them is another matter entirely.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Felix Nikolas Prehn on mortgage rates and the 10-year Treasury yield
item.description:
Felix Nikolas Prehn is an economist and former investment banker whose research examines money, asset prices and US households from 2000 to 2026. A buyer who opens a mortgage quote is looking at the last link in a chain that starts in the bond market.

The starting point for a mortgage rate

A St. Louis Fed explainer on mortgage rates names the 10-year Treasury note as the benchmark for the 30-year mortgage. Treasury securities count as very low risk because the US government backs them, so investors use their yields as the yardstick for other long-term investments.

The choice of a 10-year note for a 30-year loan comes down to how long people keep their mortgages. Many are written for 30 years, but most are paid off, refinanced or ended by the sale of the home well before then. The average life of a mortgage is much closer to 10 years.

Some banks bundle thousands of mortgages into securities and sell them to investors, who receive the principal and interest homeowners pay. Those investors compare the return on mortgage-backed securities with the return on the 10-year note. The two respond to the same signals, such as data on inflation and economic growth, and their yields often move in the same direction.

The securities are riskier than Treasuries, so investors demand a higher yield for taking that risk. The explainer calls the market value of that extra risk, plus the added costs of a mortgage (origination expenses, servicing fees and lender profit), the mortgage spread. The mortgage rate is roughly the Treasury yield plus that spread.

Movement of the two lines

Freddie Mac's weekly survey records the average rate lenders quoted on 30-year fixed loans. The Treasury Department publishes the 10-year yield each business day. Treasury data put the 10-year yield at 4.95 per cent on 10 September and 5.22 per cent on 8 October, so both lines rose over the four weeks.

Between those dates the survey logged 6.95 per cent, 7.03 per cent and 7.28 per cent in the weeks of 17 September, 24 September and 1 October. The mortgage rate did not jump in one step. It climbed week by week.

Five years earlier, the survey for 7 October 2021, showed an average 30-year rate of 2.99 per cent, and the 10-year yield that day was 1.58 per cent.

For the week of 8 October 2026, the same two readings were 7.40 per cent and 5.22 per cent.

Those are single dated readings, not a full history. The survey is an average of quotes and reflects what lenders offered that week, so an individual borrower's quote, or a rate locked earlier or later, can differ from the published figure.

The change for a buyer

A buyer who shopped for a typical 30-year loan in October 2021 faced a survey average of 2.99 per cent. A buyer who closes now meets a survey average near 7.40 per cent for the same 30 years.

A fixed-rate loan keeps the rate it was signed at for the whole term, so the higher rate reaches only the people who sign now. Owners with a 2021 loan keep paying the old rate.

The loan amount does not have to change for the monthly bill to change. Because mortgage and Treasury yields often move together, a buyer who shops in September and closes in October can see a different quote on the same house.

The same shift appears from another side for anyone saving a deposit rather than already holding a mortgage. The savings goal is attached to a loan whose rate has moved. The monthly payment depends on the mortgage rate in force at the point of signing, not only on the price of the house.

Prehn's paper on housing

The paper does not analyse how lenders price mortgages, but it examines the part of the chain that runs from interest rates to housing. Its text, available on Zenodo as a preprint since 25 September 2026, free to read and reuse with credit, describes a discount-rate channel: when the expected path for interest rates falls, long-lived assets such as housing become worth more today.

A second channel runs through credit. The paper states higher asset prices raise the borrowing capacity of people who already own assets, which finances further purchases.

Rents are where that shows up for people who do not own. The paper states housing costs feed into rents slowly, so owners have already gained by the time renters see the change.

Housing is also where the paper locates the bottom half's debt. It states that 68 per cent of that group's assets are a home or consumer durables, and that the group owes $3.2 trillion in mortgages.

About Felix Nikolas Prehn

Felix Nikolas Prehn, also known as Nikolas Prehn, is an economist and former investment banker, born in Germany. He is a tech founder: he co-founded TradeVision.io (Acetrader Inc), founded Winston Daily and The Prehn Institute, and publishes weekly on YouTube. He is also a painter and sculptor and a public advocate for animal rescue.

About The Prehn Institute

He is a tech founder: he co-founded TradeVision.io (Acetrader Inc), founded Winston Daily and The Prehn Institute, and publishes weekly on YouTube. It publishes research on the financial markets and provides instruction in professional market practice.

item.title: Where do traders get interest rate expectations for central banks?
item.description:
Interest rate expectations are among the most important drivers for financial markets. They influence government bond yields, currencies, equity valuations, and even cryptocurrencies.

But how can traders check whether the market expects a central bank to cut rates, hold them steady, or deliver rate hikes? The answer lies in interest rate derivatives, particularly overnight index swaps (OIS) and interest rate futures.

These instruments allow market participants to express views on future interest rates, hedge their exposure to changes in monetary policy, and translate market prices into implied expectations.

The market doesn't wait for a central bank meeting to form expectations about its next decision. Traders can buy and sell derivatives whose value depends on interest rates over specific future periods.

When macro or geopolitical developments change the future outlook, or central bank officials communication hints to a certain decision, traders reassess the likely path of monetary policy before the central bank takes action. They then adjust their positions in interest rate derivatives, causing prices to move.

These price movements can be translated into implied interest rates. By comparing the implied rate with the current policy rate, traders can estimate how much tightening or easing the market has priced in.

There are two main instruments for this purpose: overnight index swaps and interest rate futures.

Overnigth Index Swap (OIS)

An overnight index swap (OIS) is a derivative contract in which two parties exchange interest payments calculated using different rates. In a standard overnight indexed swap, one party pays a fixed interest rate while receiving a floating rate linked to a compounded overnight benchmark.

The relevant benchmark depends on the currency. For example, US dollar OIS commonly reference the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), while euro OIS generally reference the Euro Short-Term Rate (€STR).

Overnight rates tend to follow the central bank's policy rate closely. When the central bank changes its policy rate, the overnight rate adjusts accordingly. Therefore, the expected path of future overnight rates provides information about the market's expectations for monetary policy.

Suppose the Fed's current target range has a midpoint of 4.00%, and an OIS contract implies an average overnight rate of 3.75% over a future period. This reflects expectations of monetary easing during that period.

However, the implied rate is an average over the contract's relevant period, not necessarily the rate expected immediately after the next meeting. To isolate expectations for a specific meeting, traders use instruments and calculations tied to that meeting's date.

Short-Term Interest Rate Futures (STIR)

Short-Term Interest Rate futures (STIR) are also used to derive future interest rate expectations. These standardized, exchange-traded contracts allow traders to take positions linked to interest rates.

For example, federal funds futures are linked to the effective federal funds rate, the overnight rate in the US banking system. Their prices can be used to infer expectations for the average effective federal funds rate during a particular calendar month.

A simplified pricing convention is:

Futures price = 100 − implied interest rate

If a federal funds futures contract trades at 96.00, its implied rate is approximately 4.00% (100.00 - 96.00). If the contract price rises to 96.25, the implied rate falls to 3.75%. The relationship works in the opposite direction because higher expected interest rates generally translate into lower futures prices. This allows traders to track changes in market pricing following economic releases, inflation data, employment reports, and central bank communications.

For the ECB, traders often monitor €STR-linked futures, while SONIA-linked futures are widely used to assess expectations for the Bank of England. The exact contracts and conventions differ, but the underlying principle is similar as market prices are converted into implied interest rates, which can then be compared with the expected policy path.

Why market-implied expectations change

Interest rate expectations are continuously reassessed as new information becomes available. Say for example that an inflation report comes in significantly above expectations. Traders may conclude that inflation is proving more persistent than anticipated, making the central bank less likely to cut rates. They may then sell interest rate futures or adjust their OIS positions, pushing implied rates higher.

Conversely, a weaker than expected employment report could increase concerns about economic growth and raise the probability of monetary easing. Implied rates could then fall. Central bank communication is equally important. A speech suggesting that policymakers are becoming more concerned about inflation may lead markets to price a higher policy rate, even if the central bank does not change its current rate.

The key point is that markets react not simply to whether data are strong or weak, but to how the information changes the expected path of monetary policy. 

Where can traders find these expectations?

Traders can access market-implied interest rate expectations through several sources. Exchange websites provide futures prices and contract specifications. CME Group publishes information on federal funds futures and offers its FedWatch tool, which estimates probabilities for upcoming Fed decisions using those futures.

For the euro area and the UK, traders can examine relevant €STR- and SONIA-linked futures and swap markets through exchange data and financial market platforms. 

Bloomberg and LSEG Workspace also provide extensive interest rate derivatives data, including forward curves, swap rates, and meeting-by-meeting expectations. Specialized websites and market dashboards may present these calculations in a more accessible format. Most of these platforms are premium.

The most comprehensive free source is centralbank.watch where you can find interest rate expectations for most major central banks.

Why expectations matter more than the decision itself

The most important variable isn't the central bank's actual decision, but the difference between that decision and what was already priced in. Suppose the market expects the Fed to cut rates by 25 basis points, but the central bank leaves rates unchanged. The decision will initially appear hawkish because it is less dovish than expected and the hawkish repricing will move markets. However, the full reaction will also depend on the guidance accompanying the decision.

This is why traders monitor interest rate expectations before and after every major economic release and central bank meeting. Changes in implied rates help reveal how the market is reassessing the monetary policy outlook, which is more informative than the central bank decision itself.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: What are the main events for today?
item.description:
EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, we only have the final Eurozone CPI report. The final data is almost never market-moving because the markets react more to new information, which is given by the preliminary data. 

As a reminder, the ECB is expected to keep interest rates steady at the upcoming meeting due to lack of clear second-round effects and the recent bond market woes. Traders expect the next rate hike to come in December. 

AMERICAN SESSION

In the American session, we have lots of low-tier releases like the US industrial production and the US Import/Export prices. The industrial production data is correlated with the ISM manufacturing PMI, so there's not much new information it can give to traders.

item.title: Warsh won’t prejudge rest of 2026, names October and December as decision points
item.description:
With no guidance from the chair, short-dated Treasuries and the dollar will take their lead from data before the 27–28 October meeting, which points to bigger reactions to releases. His comment that events have broadly matched expectations leans slightly hawkish, since the September projections pointed to another hike this year. Oil remains a key input: fuel-driven inflation tied to the Iran war is the main source of upside price pressure, so moves in crude will feed directly into hike pricing. A hawkish-leaning Fed has tended to weigh on gold rather than support it.

---

Earlier, Hammack no so reticent on forward guidance:

  • Fed's Hammack questions whether Fed policy is tight enough as inflation risks build

---

Warsh came to Bangkok and said, in effect, watch the data, not me, which is exactly what he has been promising to do.

Summary:

  • Warsh said he does not believe in saying what he might do at meetings for the rest of 2026
  • He said the October and December meetings will be the crystallising moments for judging output, jobs and inflation
  • Since the September meeting, the world has broadly conformed to Fed expectations, he said
  • He called a structural investment surge the biggest upside in the global economy, crediting good policies
  • AI will hit demand before supply, will make the economy more productive over time, and has an uncertain near-term impact on jobs, he said
  • The Fed will hold a field hearing on AI in the San Francisco Bay Area on 16 November

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal the central bank’s next move on Friday. He said he does not believe in saying what he might do at meetings for the rest of 2026, and pointed to the Fed’s October and December meetings as the moments when policymakers will take stock.

Speaking at an IMF session in Bangkok, held during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, Warsh said the world has broadly conformed to the Fed’s expectations since its September policy meeting. He said the Fed has made clear it will deliver price stability, but that he does not believe in prejudging meetings. Policymakers will make their judgements at the October and December meetings, which he described as the crystallising moments for assessing output, employment and inflation.

The refusal to give guidance was no surprise. Warsh has repeatedly argued that the Fed should say less about its intentions so that markets form their own view of the economy, and he has said he opposes signalling decisions in advance. Friday’s comments put that approach [into practice](LINK TO QUIETER FED PIECE), leaving investors to rely on incoming data ahead of the 27 and 28 October meeting.

His remark that events have broadly matched expectations is still worth noting. In September the Fed raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first hike since 2023, and most officials projected at least one further increase this year. If the outlook has unfolded as expected, that suggests he sees little reason so far to depart from that path, although he stopped short of saying so.

Warsh devoted much of his remarks to investment and artificial intelligence. He described a structural investment surge, which he attributed to good policies, as the most important upside development in the global economy. On AI, he said the technology would make the economy more productive and create more wealth, but that the path would be bumpy, and that its near-term impact on employment is uncertain. He said AI is likely to boost demand before it delivers the supply-side gains that could ease inflation, and that it should also help central banks gain confidence in their data.

That sequencing matters for policy. If AI-related investment lifts spending now while productivity gains arrive later, it adds to near-term inflation pressure. That is consistent with Warsh’s earlier argument that current rates are not restricting activity.

Warsh also said the Fed’s policies spill over to the rest of the world, but that other countries’ policies spill back to the US too. He added that the Fed will hold a field hearing on AI in the San Francisco Bay Area on 16 November, as part of its task force work.

The next markers are US data ahead of the 27 and 28 October meeting, and whether other Fed officials fill the gap left by the chair’s silence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

  • Its SpaceX-developed thrusters let it flip and land; Musk claims 0–60 mph in under a second and a top speed above 230 mph

Tesla finally showed off its long-delayed new Roadster on Thursday, complete with SpaceX-developed thrusters that let the car flip itself in mid-air. Buyers will need deep pockets and plenty of patience, though, with production not due to start until 2028.

At a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, the two-seater drove upside down on a ramp, then used its built-in thrusters to turn and land. Chief Executive Elon Musk said the car can reach 60 mph from a standstill in under a second and hit a top speed above 230 mph, and suggested the production version could aim even higher. Securing a place in the queue is costly. Tesla is asking for a $5,000 deposit followed by a further $45,000 within 10 days, taking the upfront commitment to $50,000. A higher-specification version requires a $250,000 deposit. Tesla has not confirmed a price, although it is expected to exceed $250,000, well above the roughly $200,000 base price quoted when the car was first unveiled.

The timeline remains the biggest question mark. Tesla first showed a next-generation Roadster in 2017 and said deliveries would begin in 2020, before a series of delays. Thursday’s event itself came two weeks after a planned 1 October reveal was postponed by severe weather.

For investors, the Roadster is a brand statement rather than a business driver. Musk himself has played down its financial importance, and one equity analyst estimates sales of around 2,000 cars a year, a small fraction of the 1.6 million vehicles Tesla sold last year. The company’s valuation rests far more on its push into artificial intelligence, self-driving and robotics, including its Cybercab robotaxi and Optimus humanoid robots.

That makes the Roadster a halo product: one designed to show off engineering ambition and keep the brand in the headlines, rather than move the needle on earnings. ---

---

Bailey is frustrated with inflation but not yet alarmed by it, which leaves November live without giving hike-hungry markets the nod they wanted.

Summary:

  • Bailey said second-round effects from high energy prices have been subdued so far
  • He said it is too early to form strong views, and that businesses are emphasising cost-cutting
  • He called above-target UK inflation enormously frustrating
  • The UK economy is more resilient than expected but not as strong as needed, he said
  • Middle East news is the biggest factor moving gilt yields, he said
  • Bank Rate is 3.75%, after a 6-3 hold in September; the next decision is on 5 November

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said on Friday that higher energy prices have so far had only a limited knock-on effect on wider British prices, but that it is too early to form a firm view. That leaves the door open to a rate rise without signalling that one is imminent.

Speaking at the Institute of International Finance’s annual meeting in Bangkok, held alongside the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, Bailey said the evidence on so-called second-round effects has been quite subdued. These are effects where higher energy costs feed into wages and the prices of other goods and services. He added that businesses are emphasising cost-cutting, rather than passing costs on.

At the same time, Bailey described above-target UK inflation as enormously frustrating. He said the economy has proved more resilient than the Bank expected, but is not as strong as it needs to be, and that news from the Middle East is the biggest factor driving UK government bond yields.

The comments matter because markets have been betting heavily on a rate rise at the Bank’s next decision on 5 November. Bank Rate stands at 3.75%, and at the September meeting the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold, with three members preferring an immediate increase. Bailey voted with the majority. In late September, however, he warned that persistently high energy prices would make it harder to keep rates on hold, a shift in tone that helped push hike expectations higher.

Friday’s remarks are more balanced. Describing second-round effects as subdued is consistent with the Bank’s September assessment, and suggests Bailey is not yet convinced the energy shock is becoming embedded in wage and price setting. That is the key test for the MPC majority. His frustration over inflation, however, signals little tolerance for a prolonged overshoot, so the comments stop short of pushing back against a November move.

His point on gilt yields underlines how far UK rates now depend on oil and gas prices tied to the Iran war. A further rise in energy costs would strengthen the case for tightening, while an easing in Middle East tensions would weaken it.

The next markers are UK September inflation data next week, the 28 October Budget, and the Bank’s November decision, which will come with fresh forecasts.

item.title: Ethereum whale’s $13.45M loss reflects a year-long exit, not a fresh ETH dump
item.description:
Ethereum whale’s $13.45 million loss is a year-long exit, not a fresh dump

A wallet that began buying Ethereum (ETH) near last year’s market peak has now moved almost its entire position onto exchanges. On-chain analyst Ai Yi flagged the activity, Odaily reported it, and Binance News carried it on Friday. The headline figure, a potential $13.45 million loss on 15,361 ETH, checks out arithmetically. But it describes twelve months of activity, not a single sale this week, and that difference matters for how traders should read it.

What the wallet actually did

The investor started buying in September 2025 at around $4,600 and kept adding as prices fell. In total, 15,810 ETH was withdrawn from exchanges at an average cost of about $4,100, roughly $65 million. Between October 2025 and October 2026, the wallet sent 15,361 ETH back to exchanges at an average price of about $3,226. The most recent deposit came a few hours before the report, but its size was not disclosed. The wallet still holds 572 ETH.

Why a deposit is not the same as a sale

Moving coins onto an exchange often comes before selling, which is why analysts track these transfers. But on-chain data shows that coins moved, not that they were sold. Exchange deposits can also be used as collateral for borrowing or for internal transfers. The $13.45 million figure is therefore an estimate. It assumes every deposited coin was sold at the market price on the day it arrived.

The averaging-down lesson

Buying more as prices fell did bring this investor’s average cost down from about $4,600 to about $4,100. The catch is that it also grew the position while the market kept falling. Ethereum has since dropped well below both levels. ETH was consolidating around $2,500 on October 12, after sliding from roughly $2,725 on October 5 to around $2,474 on October 9.

My read is that the gradual exit limited the damage. Holding the full position until today, at roughly $2,500 per coin, would have meant a paper loss of about $1,600 per ETH, or around $24.6 million. The broader point for readers is that averaging down only helps if the asset eventually recovers. Without a plan for when to stop adding, it can turn a mistimed entry into a much larger one.

Putting one whale in context

This wallet’s selling is small next to the flows moving through Ethereum ETFs. Its full year of deposits, about 15,361 ETH, is less than the roughly 22,440 ETH that left BlackRock’s ETHA in a single day on October 9. kucoin

Those fund flows have been heavy:

  • Investors pulled about $542 million from US spot Ethereum ETFs in the week ending October 9, which was described as the largest weekly outflow since January. cryptobriefingcoinstats
  • Ethereum funds lost a further $85.4 million on October 12. kucoin

A caution on reading those numbers: ETF outflows are net redemptions and do not necessarily mean all of the underlying ETH was sold on the open market. Like the whale’s deposits, they show money leaving, not exactly where the coins ended up.

What could change the interpretation

The story rests on the analyst correctly identifying the wallet. If those addresses turn out to belong to a custodian, fund or exchange-linked entity, the “underwater investor” framing falls away. On the other hand, if several wallets that bought near the 2025 highs show the same pattern, that would point to wider capitulation among late buyers, not one person’s exit. Capitulation here means holders giving up and selling at a loss.

What to watch next

  • The remaining 572 ETH: if they move to an exchange, the wallet’s exit is complete.
  • Other high-cost holders: look for similar deposit patterns among wallets that bought in the $4,000 to $4,800 range.
  • ETF flows and price together: if ETF outflows ease and ETH holds near $2,500, that would suggest selling pressure is fading. If outflows continue and price keeps slipping, late buyers may still be heading for the exits.

The practical takeaway is to treat single-whale headlines as a prompt to check flows and price, not as a signal on their own. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Google’s 40-fold quantum leap: big for Willow, smaller for Alphabet’s share price
item.description:
The result is a research milestone rather than a revenue event, so any lasting effect on Alphabet shares is likely to be limited, given the company’s value rests mainly on search, cloud and AI. Smaller pure-play quantum stocks are more sensitive to sector headlines and could see sharper sentiment-driven moves. The encryption angle may resurface in crypto markets, but the gap between this result and what code-breaking would require is wide. The bigger signal is competitive: it strengthens Google’s standing in the race for error-corrected quantum computing.

-

Google has made quantum computing’s most expensive ingredient much cheaper to cook, but it is still working in a test kitchen, not a factory.

Summary:

  • Google says magic state cultivation cut errors about 40-fold on its Willow chip
  • The result, published in Science, produced magic states with 99.99% fidelity
  • Magic states are a key bottleneck, with some estimates putting their production cost at up to 95% of machine capacity
  • The test used at most 54 of Willow’s 105 qubits, and only about 8% of attempts passed every check
  • Google says larger-scale demonstrations are still needed and has given no timeline
  • Breaking RSA-2048 encryption would need magic states about a million times cleaner

Google says it has demonstrated a way around one of the biggest bottlenecks in quantum computing, cutting errors in a crucial resource by about 40-fold on its Willow chip. The result brings practical, error-corrected machines a step closer but stops well short of making them a near-term reality.

The company’s Quantum AI team set out the work in a paper published in the journal Science and a blog post on Thursday. It centres on so-called magic states, a special type of quantum state that quantum computers need to carry out the full range of calculations that would make them useful. Producing high-quality magic states has been extremely costly, with some estimates suggesting it could take up as much as 95% of a machine’s capacity.

Google’s approach, called magic state cultivation, was proposed by its own researchers in 2024 but had until now been tested only in theory and simulation. It works by growing a rough magic state in a small section of the chip and running repeated error checks, discarding any attempt in which a flaw is detected. On Willow, the technique cut errors by roughly 40 times compared with states produced without it, and delivered magic states with a fidelity of 99.99%.

The significance lies in efficiency. If magic states can be made cheaply and reliably, more of a future quantum computer’s capacity can be devoted to actual calculations, reducing the size and cost of machines needed to solve useful problems.

The caveats are substantial. The experiment used at most 54 of Willow’s 105 qubits, and only about 8% of cultivation attempts passed every check. Google itself said the method still needs to be proven at larger scale and that many technical challenges remain, and it gave no timeline for commercially useful machines.

The result also feeds into the debate over quantum risks to encryption, including the cryptography that protects bitcoin and online banking. For now that risk remains distant: breaking widely used RSA-2048 encryption would require magic states roughly a million times cleaner than those Google has produced.

For investors, the announcement is a research milestone rather than a commercial one, and it is unlikely to change the outlook for Alphabet, whose value rests mainly on search, cloud and artificial intelligence. It does reinforce Google’s position in the race to build error-corrected quantum computers. Headlines like this have tended to drive sharp moves in smaller, pure-play quantum stocks.

The next markers will be whether Google can show cultivation working at larger scale, and whether independent researchers confirm the results. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman: Warsh’s quieter Fed: why less guidance could mean more market volatility
item.description:
Less forward guidance shifts the burden onto data, which points to bigger moves in short-dated Treasuries, the dollar and rate-sensitive equities around key releases, as this week’s CPI reaction showed. Bond volatility may stay elevated even if the eventual Fed path matches the consensus for a single December hike. Oil is a central variable in that regime: with the Iran war keeping energy costs high, every swing in crude feeds directly into inflation expectations, and with less Fed guidance to anchor them, into rate pricing. Gold is likely to keep trading off yields and hike expectations rather than geopolitical headlines.

---

Warsh wants markets to stop staring at the Fed and start reading the economy, but after 15 years of hand-holding, the first steps without guidance may be wobbly ones.

Summary:

  • Warsh has set up five task forces, including one on communications, and wants the Fed to reveal less of its internal thinking
  • He opposes giving guidance on upcoming rate decisions
  • Goldman’s Investment Strategy Group expects changes to be gradual, but flags concerns about longer policy lags and extra volatility
  • Rate pricing has already swung sharply on data, including a slump in October hike odds in late September and a jump in yields after this week’s CPI
  • Most major banks expect one more Fed hike in December
  • Warsh speaks in Bangkok on Friday, ahead of the 27–28 October FOMC meeting

For more than a decade, investors have been trained to read the Federal Reserve’s every word. Kevin Warsh wants to break the habit, and Goldman Sachs is warning clients that weaning markets off Fed guidance could come with a price: longer policy lags and more volatility.

The Fed chair, who speaks at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday, has set up five task forces to review how the central bank works. They cover communications, the balance sheet, data sources, productivity and jobs, and the inflation framework. Communications is the one most likely to change how markets trade. Warsh has argued that the Fed should say less about its internal thinking so that investors form their own view of the economy, likening it to watching the game rather than the official. He has also said he opposes giving guidance on whether the Fed will hike, cut or hold at upcoming meetings.

In its latest quarterly update for clients, Goldman’s Investment Strategy Group said any changes from the task forces are likely to be gradual. But it flagged a concern shared by some investors. If the Fed tells markets less, it may take longer for policy to work through financial conditions, and the adjustment could be bumpier for both markets and the real economy.

The logic is straightforward. Forward guidance has long worked as a policy tool in its own right. When the Fed signals its path, bond yields, mortgage rates and the dollar move ahead of any decision, doing part of the tightening or easing in advance. Take the signals away and markets must wait for the data, and for the decisions themselves, to adjust. That could mean bigger moves on key releases and more frequent repricing between meetings.

There are early signs of what that looks like. In the space of a week in late September, futures pricing for an October hike swung from around 70% to below 40% as softer inflation data and comments from a senior Fed official changed the picture. Goldman itself pushed back its expected next hike from October to December at the start of the month. This week’s hotter-than-expected consumer price data then lifted Treasury yields sharply as traders added to bets on further tightening.

The September hike, the first since 2023, came with a statement that offered no explicit guidance on future moves. That leaves markets leaning heavily on data and on individual officials, with regional presidents such as Cleveland’s Beth Hammack filling some of the gap with their own views.

Warsh’s case has merit. Heavy guidance can lock a central bank into a path that the data no longer support, and can encourage markets to bet on the Fed rather than on the economy. A market that does its own homework may also price risk more honestly. The trade-off is that the transition period, while investors relearn how to read the economy without a script, is likely to be noisier.

For traders, that suggests a regime in which economic releases matter more and Fed meetings matter differently. Short-dated Treasuries, the dollar and rate-sensitive equities are likely to be the most exposed. Bond volatility may stay elevated even if the Fed’s path ends up close to what Wall Street expects, with most major banks now forecasting a single further hike in December.

Friday’s appearance in Bangkok is a test case. If Warsh sticks to his script and offers little on October, markets will have to make their own call before the Fed meets on 27 and 28 October, which is exactly the point. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
