item.title: Trump draws two red lines on Iran but keeps Pickaxe Mountain strike in play
item.description:
The remarks are unlikely to move oil much on their own, since they repeat earlier positions, but they reinforce the geopolitical risk premium in crude by keeping a strike on Iran’s remaining nuclear infrastructure on the table. The real oil risk lies in Hormuz: any escalation that triggers further Iranian attacks on tankers would tighten already constrained flows and push prices back above $100. Ruling out nuclear weapons and ground troops slightly reduces tail risk, while Trump’s pre-midterm pause offers near-term breathing room. As throughout the conflict, higher oil feeds inflation and Fed hike expectations, which has weighed on gold rather than lifting it.

--

Trump has taken nukes and boots off the table, but not the bombers, and for oil traders the mountain near Natanz is still on the map.

Summary:

  • Trump told Newsmax he would not use nuclear weapons on Iran and does not see US troops on the ground there
  • He said the US may have to go after Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site near Natanz linked to Iran’s nuclear programme
  • He said he is talking to Russia and China about denuclearisation, without giving details
  • Last week, Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the November midterms
  • CBS News has reported US plans to use a massive conventional bomb against Iranian military sites if ordered
  • Hormuz disruption and tanker attacks keep US crude near $97, despite accelerated IEA stock releases

US President Donald Trump said he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran and did not expect to send ground troops into the country. He kept open the possibility of a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, the underground site near Natanz that analysts link to Iran’s nuclear programme.

Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, Trump said the US may have to go after Pickaxe Mountain. He also said he was talking to Russia and China about denuclearisation, though he gave no detail on those discussions.

Pickaxe Mountain, known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang, is a complex of tunnels built into a mountain a few miles from Natanz. Iran declared it a centrifuge assembly site in 2021, and analysts estimate it is buried about 100 metres underground. It is widely described as the last significant nuclear-linked site in Iran to have escaped strikes, and Trump has repeatedly threatened to hit it since July. Analysts have cautioned that even the heaviest US bunker-busting bombs may not guarantee its destruction.

The comments add to mixed signals from Washington. Last week Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections in early November and pointed to productive conversations with Tehran. At the same time, CBS News has reported that the White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use one of the largest US conventional bombs against military sites in Iran, should the president order it. Ruling out nuclear weapons and ground troops narrows the range of options, but leaves air strikes on the table.

For energy markets, the key question is what any escalation would mean for the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of the world’s oil normally passes. Traffic through the strait has been severely disrupted during the conflict, and Iranian attacks on tankers have increased in recent weeks. US crude traded near $97 a barrel on Thursday, close to the $100 mark. Supply concerns kept prices elevated despite moves by IEA members to speed up releases of emergency oil stocks.

The remarks are unlikely to shift oil prices much on their own, since they largely restate positions Trump has taken before. But they suggest a strike on Iran’s remaining nuclear infrastructure remains a live option once the pre-election pause ends, keeping a geopolitical risk premium in crude.

The next markers will be any sign of progress in contacts with Tehran before the midterms, further attacks on shipping in Hormuz, and whether Washington’s stated pause holds. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6947 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary:
  • The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets. 
  • China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours. 
  • The midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the prior day's close, moves in major currencies, broader international FX conditions and domestic factors such as capital flows and growth momentum, with policymakers retaining discretion over the final number. 
  • If market pressure pushes the yuan toward either edge of the band, the PBOC can intervene through direct buying or selling of yuan, liquidity adjustments, or guidance via state-owned banks. 
  • A stronger-than-expected fixing typically signals the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can indicate tolerance for a softer currency or discomfort with the pace of gains. 
  • For nearly a year the fixing has been set weaker than market estimates, with the gap reaching its widest since February in late August. 
  • In September the PBOC strengthened the fixing for eight straight sessions, the longest run since 2023, and the midpoint reached its strongest level since February 2023. 
  • The yuan has pushed to its strongest levels since early 2023 onshore and since mid-2022 offshore, with Goldman Sachs expecting Beijing to remain comfortable with sustained but gradual appreciation. 
The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.The timing has been linked to diplomacy. The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: India curbs gold ETF buying before Diwali, removing a seasonal prop for gold demand
item.description:
The curbs trim a traditional seasonal support for gold just as Indian festive demand would normally pick up. That adds to pressure on prices, which have already been weighed down by rising expectations of further US rate hikes rather than lifted by geopolitical risk. Physical buying through jewellers is unaffected, so the hit to overall Indian demand may be limited, but the ETF channel has been a growing source of fresh investment flows. Oil remains the root cause: higher crude prices have swollen India’s import bill and weakened the rupee, so a sustained move in oil will shape how long the restrictions stay in place.

--- India wants its citizens to celebrate Diwali with a little less gold, and the bullion market loses one of its more dependable autumn buyers.

Summary:

  • Kotak Mahindra, UTI and HDFC mutual funds are among those suspending bulk subscriptions to gold ETFs
  • The halt reportedly followed discussions with market regulator SEBI, and redemptions are unaffected
  • The move comes ahead of Dussehra and Diwali, the peak season for gold buying in India
  • The rupee has been pressured by higher oil prices and foreign equity selling, and gold and silver import duties were raised earlier this year
  • Gold imports fell to $1.8 billion in September from $2.3 billion in August
  • A bullion dealer called the move a precaution against an October import surge

Gold faces the loss of one of its most reliable seasonal supports after several large Indian mutual funds suspended bulk subscriptions to gold exchange-traded funds, just as the country enters its peak buying season for the metal.

Fund houses including Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, UTI Mutual Fund and HDFC Mutual Fund issued public notices late on Thursday halting bulk purchases of their gold ETFs, Reuters reported. The notices gave no reason, and redemptions remain unaffected. A mutual fund executive and two bullion industry officials told Reuters the move followed discussions with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator. SEBI did not respond to a request for comment outside business hours.

The timing matters for gold. India is the world’s second-largest consumer of the metal and relies on imports for most of its supply. Demand typically rises around Dussehra in October and Diwali in early November, when buying gold is considered auspicious. Inflows into gold and silver ETFs surged during last year’s festive season as investors sought alternatives to lacklustre equity returns.

The underlying concern is the rupee. The currency has been under pressure this year from higher oil prices, which have swollen the import bill, and from heavy foreign selling of Indian shares. Strong gold demand has added to the strain, prompting the government to raise import duties on gold and silver earlier this year. Several fund houses also capped large gold ETF investments in June as authorities sought to curb imports.

The move appears pre-emptive rather than a response to a current surge. Gold imports fell to $1.8 billion in September from $2.3 billion in August. A bullion dealer at a private bank told Reuters that imports had not added to the trade deficit in recent months, and described the halt as a precaution against a jump in imports during October.

For the gold market, the curbs remove a source of incremental demand at a time when prices have already been under pressure from rising expectations of further US interest rate increases. Retail investors can still buy physical gold, so festive demand will not disappear. However, limiting large ETF purchases narrows one channel that has added fresh buying in past seasons.

The key questions now are whether other fund houses follow, how long the suspensions last, and whether India’s October import figures show festive demand shifting into physical gold instead. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nike’s problem is demand, not tariffs: what Moody’s warning really signals
item.description:
Reading the outlook change as a demand story rather than a tariff story is a more negative signal for Nike shares, because demand problems tend to last longer and cannot be fixed by a shift in trade policy. Credit investors are likely to stay calm while the A2 rating holds, but a sustained run of falling earnings would put the rating itself in play. China-exposed consumer brands may face closer scrutiny, given the scale of Nike’s slump there. The 16–17 November investor day is the next catalyst for both the shares and the debt.

---

A year ago Moody’s worried about what tariffs would cost Nike, but now it is worried about whether shoppers, especially in China, will come back.

Summary:

  • Moody’s cited a longer turnaround and Nike’s strategic actions, not tariffs, in changing its outlook to negative
  • In 2025, Moody’s cut Nike to A2 on tariff cost pressure, with a stable outlook
  • Nike’s revenue fell about 4% last quarter, with Greater China down 26% in constant currency and Converse down 28%
  • Gross margin rose slightly, with no tariff hit quantified
  • The Pace restructuring carries about $1 billion of charges, with most savings arriving in fiscal 2029 and 2030
  • New duties on China and Vietnam goods are a future risk, and investor day on 16–17 November is the next marker

When Moody’s changed its outlook on Nike to negative this week, the obvious suspect was tariffs. A closer look at the agency’s reasoning and at Nike’s own latest results points somewhere else. The pressure on earnings is coming mainly from weak demand and the cost of the company’s turnaround, with tariffs a risk ahead rather than the main driver so far.

That distinction marks a shift from a year ago. When Moody’s cut Nike’s rating to A2 from A1 in 2025, it cited cost pressure from higher tariffs and moved the outlook to stable. This time, in its outlook change on Nike, the agency pointed instead to a turnaround taking longer than expected, falling revenue and earnings into fiscal 2028, and the drag from Nike’s own strategic actions.

Nike’s first-quarter figures support that reading. Revenue fell about 4% and missed forecasts, with sales in Greater China down 26% on a currency-neutral basis and the Converse brand down 28%. Nike’s direct-to-consumer business, including digital, also shrank. Yet the gross margin rose slightly, helped by lower logistics costs and currency moves, and the company did not quantify any tariff hit in the quarter. A tariff-driven squeeze would usually show up in margins first. Here the damage is in sales.

Part of the weakness is deliberate. Nike has been cutting back on discount-led online and off-price sales to rebuild the brand’s pricing power, which shrinks revenue in the short term by design. It has also launched a restructuring programme called Pace. Pace carries about $1 billion of charges and is expected to deliver around $2.5 billion of savings, with most of the benefit not arriving until fiscal 2029 and 2030. That timetable lines up closely with Moody’s expectation of pressure into fiscal 2028.

Tariffs have not disappeared from the picture. Nike benefited from a refund of nearly $1 billion after earlier tariffs were struck down, but new duties of 12.5% on goods from China and Vietnam took effect in late July and barely touched the latest quarter. Nike’s guidance cites higher input costs, so tariffs could add pressure from here.

The split matters for how investors read the story. Tariff costs can ease with a policy change, but demand problems, particularly in China, take longer to fix and depend on Nike winning back consumers. The partial offset is that some of the revenue decline is a choice, making this partly a managed reset rather than pure weakness.

Nike’s investor day on 16 and 17 November is the next marker. It will show whether management can set out a credible path back to growth, especially in China. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Two AI signals, one week: TSMC’s boom and Dell’s doubts show where demand really is
item.description:
The split favours companies supplying the largest cloud and AI spenders, such as chipmakers and advanced manufacturing, over hardware makers relying on broad corporate demand. That divergence is likely to persist in stock performance until enterprise orders show clearer growth. Memory prices are the swing factor: a levelling off would pressure hardware revenue, while continued strength would delay the reckoning. Upcoming results from the biggest cloud providers are the next major catalyst, since any sign of slowing AI budgets would undermine the bullish half of the picture.

The AI boom has not cracked. It has just revealed a split: the hyperscalers are spending as hard as ever, while corporate IT departments are still deciding.

Summary:

  • TSMC beat forecasts and raised its outlook, saying AI demand is extremely robust and outrunning supply
  • Barclays downgraded Dell, HPE and NetApp, arguing enterprise AI spending has not yet inflected
  • Barclays says higher memory prices, not demand, are flattering hardware revenue
  • The two views reflect different customer bases: hyperscalers versus ordinary businesses
  • The divergence points to concentrated rather than broad AI demand
  • Hyperscaler results, memory prices and enterprise orders are the markers to watch

Two of this week’s biggest technology stories appear to send opposite messages about artificial intelligence. Taken together, they suggest the AI boom is real but narrower than some valuations assume. Demand is concentrated among the largest cloud and AI companies rather than spreading evenly through corporate IT budgets.

The bullish signal came from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world’s largest contract chipmaker. Its third-quarter profit rose nearly 70%, it raised its full-year growth outlook, and Chief Executive C.C. Wei said AI demand remained extremely robust with no sign of a slowdown. High-performance computing, the segment that includes AI accelerators, now makes up more than two-thirds of TSMC’s revenue, and the company says supply still falls well short of demand.

The cautious signal came a day earlier from Barclays. In its downgrade of Dell, the bank argued that enterprise AI spending has yet to show a meaningful inflection. It said strong revenue at hardware makers owes much to higher memory chip prices being passed on to customers. Barclays applied the same reasoning to Hewlett Packard Enterprise and NetApp, and the selloff spread across AI hardware stocks.

These views are less contradictory than they look. TSMC’s customers are dominated by the chip designers supplying the largest cloud providers and AI developers, whose spending remains heavy. Dell and its peers depend more on ordinary businesses building their own AI capacity, which is where Barclays sees the gap between expectation and reality.

The distinction matters for investors. If AI demand is concentrated at the top, the companies supplying the biggest spenders are on firmer ground than those relying on broad corporate adoption. It also means part of the recent revenue growth in enterprise hardware reflects pricing rather than volume, which could reverse if memory prices level off.

There are reasons for caution on both sides. Concentrated demand depends on a small number of very large buyers continuing to spend, while enterprise adoption could still accelerate as businesses move from experiments to deployment. Neither trend is settled.

Several markers will help resolve the debate:

  • Hyperscaler spending plans: upcoming quarterly results from the largest cloud providers will show whether their AI budgets are still rising.
  • Memory prices: a levelling off would test how much hardware revenue growth is genuine demand.
  • Enterprise orders: hardware makers’ own results will show whether AI server sales are broadening beyond a handful of large customers.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: Dell shares slide 17% in two days as Barclays questions enterprise AI demand
item.description:
The follow-through selling puts AI hardware tied to enterprise demand under sustained pressure, with servers, storage and networking stocks most exposed. The call does not dispute spending by the largest cloud and AI companies, leaving chipmakers and hyperscaler suppliers on firmer ground. Memory prices are the key sensitivity: any sign they are levelling off would strengthen the bearish case for hardware revenue. With Dell still up sharply this year, positioning remains crowded, which raises the risk of further profit-taking until the company’s own results give investors fresh evidence.

---

Updating this, all intertwined with the tech sell off of course. 

---

Barclays asked whether Dell’s customers are buying more or just paying more for memory, and two days and 17% later, the market is still voting with its feet.

Summary:

  • Dell shares fell about 11% on Wednesday and about 7% on Thursday, a two-day drop of roughly 17%
  • The stock closed Thursday near $473, nearly 20% below its mid-September record
  • Barclays cut Dell to equal weight from overweight and its target to $574 from $603
  • HPE and NetApp were also downgraded to equal weight
  • Barclays argues higher memory prices, not enterprise AI demand, are lifting hardware revenue
  • Dell has still nearly quadrupled this year, despite the selloff

Shares of Dell Technologies extended their slide on Thursday, falling about 7% after an 11% drop on Wednesday. Investors were digesting a Barclays downgrade arguing that the company’s booming revenue owes more to rising memory chip prices than to a genuine pickup in business spending on artificial intelligence.

The two-day decline of roughly 17% took the stock to around $473 at Thursday’s close. That leaves Dell nearly 20% below its record close in mid-September, close to the threshold many investors use to define a bear market. Thursday’s losses came early, with the shares opening sharply lower and briefly trading down nearly 11% before recovering some ground.

Barclays analyst Tim Long cut Dell to equal weight from overweight and lowered his price target to $574 from $603. He also downgraded Hewlett Packard Enterprise and NetApp to equal weight, applying a similar argument across enterprise hardware.

The core of the Barclays case is that enterprise AI spending has yet to show a meaningful inflection. Instead, Long argued, much of the recent strength in hardware makers’ results reflects higher memory costs being passed through to customers. That lifts reported revenue without a matching rise in underlying demand. If memory prices normalise or fall, that support could fade and leave revenue exposed.

The selloff follows an extraordinary run. Even after two days of heavy losses, Dell shares have nearly quadrupled this year, leaving little room for disappointment. The timing also creates a sharp contrast with the company’s own message. A day before the downgrade, Chief Executive Michael Dell said enterprise AI demand was only just beginning and that demand for AI computing still exceeded supply.

The pressure spread across AI hardware, with server maker Super Micro Computer and networking group Arista Networks among the stocks that weakened, while the broader technology sector posted more modest losses. That pattern suggests investors treated the call as a warning about one corner of the AI trade, hardware tied to enterprise demand, rather than a verdict on AI spending as a whole. 

The follow-through selling on Thursday matters. A one-day drop on a downgrade can reflect a quick repricing, but a second day of heavy losses suggests investors are reassessing how much of Dell’s growth is durable. The next test will be Dell’s own results and guidance. They should show whether AI server orders are broadening across enterprise customers, and how much of its revenue growth comes from pricing rather than volume. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: TSMC profit jumps nearly 70% on AI demand, but margin outlook weighs on shares
item.description:
The results (released Thursday afternoon, Taiwan time) reinforce the AI investment theme for Asian chip and hardware stocks, with TSMC’s view that demand is outrunning capacity supportive for suppliers across the semiconductor supply chain. The share reaction shows how high expectations are, though: a beat alone is no longer enough, and investors are now trading margins and cash flow. Taiwan’s equity benchmark, where TSMC carries a heavy weighting, is likely to take its lead from how the stock trades in Taipei. Higher planned capital spending is a positive read-through for equipment makers.

---

Background:

  • TSMC set for sixth straight record profit as AI demand lifts Q3 earnings

---

TSMC delivered the AI boom in numbers and told investors it is not slowing, but with the beat priced in, the market chose to fret about margins and the bill for all those new fabs.

Summary:

  • Q3 net profit rose nearly 70% to about NT$763 billion, slightly above LSEG consensus
  • Revenue of about $47 billion beat the top of TSMC’s own guidance range
  • The gross margin was about 66%, down from Q2 on the early 2nm ramp
  • AI-heavy high-performance computing made up 68% of revenue, and 2nm reached 8% of wafer revenue
  • Q4 guidance is about $52 billion to $54 billion in revenue, with 2026 growth now seen at around 44%
  • 2026 capex was reaffirmed at $60 billion to $64 billion, and US-listed shares slipped after the results

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reported a jump of nearly 70% in third-quarter net profit on Thursday and raised its full-year growth outlook, as demand for chips used in artificial intelligence showed no sign of easing. The results still failed to lift its shares, with investors focusing on softer margin guidance and a heavy spending programme.

Net profit rose to about NT$763 billion, slightly ahead of analyst estimates compiled by LSEG. Revenue reached about $47 billion, above the top of the company’s own guidance range. The gross margin of about 66% was well up on a year earlier but down from the second quarter. TSMC attributed the sequential dip mainly to the early ramp-up of its 2-nanometre production.

The shift towards AI is clear in the revenue mix. High-performance computing, the segment that includes AI accelerators, accounted for 68% of revenue, up from 57% a year earlier. The newest 2-nanometre technology made up 8% of wafer revenue, up from 3% in the previous quarter.

Chief Executive C.C. Wei said AI demand remained extremely robust and suggested it would probably outpace the company’s earlier long-term growth forecast. He said supply still falls well short of demand, with TSMC building close to 20 new fabs, most of them in Taiwan.

For the fourth quarter, TSMC guided revenue of about $52 billion to $54 billion and a gross margin of 65% to 67%, a midpoint slightly below the third quarter. It now expects full-year revenue growth of around 44% in US dollar terms, up from slightly above 40% in July. The company reaffirmed 2026 capital spending of $60 billion to $64 billion. It said investment over the next three years would be significantly higher than in the previous three.

Those last two points explain the muted market reaction. Margin guidance implies further dilution from the 2-nanometre ramp, while management said overseas factories, including in Arizona and Japan, will weigh more heavily on margins over time. Heavier capital spending also points to lower free cash flow in the near term. With strong growth already expected, the profit beat was not large enough to offset those concerns.

The longer-term message remains firmly positive for the AI supply chain. TSMC’s view that demand is running ahead of capacity, and its willingness to keep spending to meet it, suggests the investment cycle has further to run. The next tests are whether margins stabilise as 2-nanometre production matures, and whether customers’ AI spending plans hold up through next year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Moody’s cuts Nike outlook to negative, sees earnings falling into fiscal 2028
item.description:
The outlook change is a modest negative for Nike’s bonds and adds to pressure on the shares, though the affirmed A2 rating limits any immediate impact on borrowing costs. The extended timeline for falling revenue and earnings is the more market-relevant signal, because it challenges expectations of a near-term recovery. A negative outlook raises the risk of a future downgrade, which would matter more for credit investors if earnings fail to stabilise. Broader consumer discretionary names may also face scrutiny over how long restructuring costs weigh on profits.

-

Moody’s has not downgraded Nike, but by pushing its recovery out to fiscal 2028 it has put a timer on how long the turnaround can drag before the rating follows.

Summary:

  • Moody’s changed Nike’s outlook to negative and affirmed its A2 rating
  • The agency said the turnaround is taking longer than it previously expected
  • It expects revenue and earnings to fall through the fiscal year ending May 2027 and into fiscal 2028
  • Nike’s strategic actions are expected to pressure earnings over that period
  • That pressure is expected to constrain Nike’s credit metrics

Moody’s Ratings has revised its outlook on Nike to negative while affirming the sportswear group’s A2 credit rating, citing a turnaround that is taking longer than the agency had previously expected.

In a statement released on Thursday, Moody’s said it expects Nike’s revenue and earnings to decline through the fiscal year ending in May 2027 and into fiscal 2028. It added that the company’s strategic actions are likely to weigh on earnings over that period, which would constrain its credit metrics.

The decision stops short of a downgrade. An A2 rating sits in the upper-medium tier of investment grade, and affirming it signals that Moody’s still views Nike’s credit profile as solid. A negative outlook, however, indicates the agency sees a greater chance that the rating could be lowered if performance does not improve as expected. Outlook changes of this kind are typically reviewed over the following 12 to 18 months.

The key message for investors lies in the timeline. By extending its expectation of falling sales and profits well into fiscal 2028, Moody’s is effectively signalling that the recovery in Nike’s business is further away than it had assumed. The emphasis on strategic actions suggests the costs of repositioning the business, rather than any single external shock, are a central part of the pressure on earnings.

For bondholders, the move is more of a warning than an immediate change in risk, since the rating itself is unchanged. For equity investors, it adds an independent voice to concerns about how long the turnaround will take. It also puts more weight on upcoming quarterly results as evidence of whether the business is stabilising.

The next test will be Nike’s own guidance and trading updates. They will show whether revenue declines are narrowing or, as Moody’s expects, continuing beyond the current financial year. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
